utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Unfortunately Judge Kwon encountered a major obstacle on his way to the Tribunal this morning, and he told us it's better that we start and then he will join us when the sky has cleared up and he can come over. I notice that Mr. Nikolic is still not with us. I take it that we still have in force his declaration that he would like the proceedings to continue in his absence? Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The rest of the accused are here. Mr. Ostojic is not here. Will he be joining us in the course of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ostojic also has some difficulties getting here like Judge Kwon. We hope he will be here today or tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. And the Prosecution it is Mr. Nicholls and Mr. McCloskey. I see no one else. All right. This is witness number 67, I take it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal I welcome you as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you start giving evidence you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will testify the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of our solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have granted you three protective measures. One is the use of a pseudonym instead of your usual name. The other one is facial distortion, and last but not least the voice distortion. I take it these have been explained to you? I just want a confirmation from you that they are to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, will be examining you, and after that you will be cross-examined by members of the various Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. If you could look at this pseudonym sheet, PO2370 and tell us if that's you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could go into private session for his personal details and if I could sit down to -- so it will help me turn this machine off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are already in private session, and you may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. First of all, can you tell us your year of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I was born in 1962 in a village called Brnjik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it's in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- briefly outline your educational background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I completed elementary and secondary technical, or electro-technical school in Tuzla. After that I attended technical school in Tuzla and I finished, or completed my degree, I think in 1990. And I became a teacher for technical education subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And had you had an interest in ham radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. As a child I began to work as a ham radio operator. I think when I was in class 7 or 8 and this went on until a few years ago, because I really have no more time for that, so I stopped with these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In 19 -- in July 1995 what -- what letter rating had you reached with -- with the ham radio organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I had B category certification in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, my note indicates you finished electro-technical high school in 1981. Is that correct? Because I heard 1991. I may have some -- something wrong.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Maybe it states there that I received my diploma at university in Tuzla in 1991. My higher education, I think, was completed in 1991, but I'm not quite sure. My university degree was what I received then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what year or years did you do your compulsory JNA work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: 1980 to 1981. No, no, excuse me, it was from 1981 to 1982, because I completed the electoral engineering school in 1981, and immediately after that I went to serve my military term of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And briefly tell us what you did in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I was in a unit in the JNA which was anti-tank warfare units, so I was trained as a rocket operator for anti-tank missiles, guided missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after your JNA service, did -- what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The same year when I returned from the JNA I began to work in the State Security Service. This was in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you stay employed in the State Security Service through -- well, up until the war began in Bosnia in 1992 and then continued to be state security for the BiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, from 1982 until today I have been working in the same service, which changed names in that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what is your -- what is your occupation today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I am performing technical duties also now in that same service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 1994. Did you -- were you part of the formation of a -- of a group of state security interceptors that was formed (redacted) -- in about I believe December 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I didn't have any part in the forming of that service, but this was done according to the classification in the State Security Service, so I had the option of having(redacted) people join that department. So this is what was done in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you the head of that department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. It just happened that I was the head of the department, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: (redacted):

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you went to work at the northern site, was there an army unit there doing the same kind of work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the -- the techniques and the equipment that the army was using to intercept radio communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was your group doing the same kind of work using this -- roughly the same equipment and the same techniques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So I will not go into the -- all the detail of those various things, but I'll try to concentrate on perhaps some of the differences between the -- the work you were doing and the work the army was doing. So let me first ask you, you've told us how many people there were. Can you tell me what kind of shift regimen you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were two people in each shift. I had four men. I was mostly there very often. There were two-person shifts that lasted from five to seven days, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what kind of room or rooms did you work in when the work was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Since this was a military facility, we were using their infrastructure, security, food, all the things that we could not provide ourselves. They gave us one room in that facility which we worked in and we practically slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us how many sets of equipment you had in that one room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were three sets of equipment. Later we added one more teleprinter in order to control the teleprinter traffic, and then we had the opportunity of using some hand-held radio sets, but I wouldn't really count them in. So we really had three sets of equipment when we were talking about scanning and intercepting the radio relay routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that for the period of July 1995, you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period of that whole year. The whole 1995, we can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what those -- each of those sets of equipment did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. We had several antenna systems, if we can call that that, and they reached the room and then we had equipment that received the signals divided it or distributed into channels, and then were connected to the recording devices, the so-called UHER devices. That would be a brief description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what in particular, if you did have a particular area of concern, what were you listening for, what types of enemy communications or what part of the enemy were you listening for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Since we were a civilian intelligence and security organisation, we were there to collect intelligence relating to that service, but we did not ignore information that we received via our devices, so we recorded other things too. We were mostly focused on that area, but then we were also monitoring the radio range. We would find a very interesting frequency to us, and I think that was the one that we exploited the most, and that was the frequency of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say you were a civilian organisation interested in civilian work, what does that mean? What -- were you listening to civilians from the enemy as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were civilians on those routes too, and since this route that I mentioned, the frequency of the Main Staff was there, there were, by the nature of things, many pieces of information there that were useful to my service. We also had the possibility of listening to hand-held radio stations, portable or mobile telephones, and we picked up information that was important to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what the two men would do as they first -- if they'd heard over the scanners an interesting conversation, what would the two then do? Just start that process for us briefly and take us through to the -- to the end.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were two men sitting in a room at a large desk where the equipment sets were placed and if a conversation would occur at the same moment they would depress the pause button and begin recording the conversations they would be directly listening to the conversation and after this if the conversation was urgent, it would be transcribed from the UHER, it would be transferred to a free UHER and a second operator would continue to reproduce that conversation while the operator would continue to listen for possible new conversations and record them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How would the conversation that had been recorded on the UHER be reproduced, in what format or what way was it taken off the UHER?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were two ways of doing it. Mostly if the conversation was recorded well and could be audible, then it would be reproduced directly into the computer. If not, we would then do that on a piece of paper. We would conduct a reproduction, we would play it back, listen to it, we would slow it down and so on and so forth, and after that it would be typed in. That report would be typed into the computer, encrypted and sent to our base or our centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who generally typed the transcript of the intercept into the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were all trained to do that. When we are talking about these two people in the shift, the person who was the quicker typist would usually type it into the computer, at that point of time. But this wasn't a rule, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the conversation was taken down on pieces of paper before being typed into the computer, what was done with those pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: After collecting a few of these on the desk then we would just go behind the building and burn them. They were not important to us anymore because then we would receive confirmation that our reports had already been received by the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who sent off the reports that were put into the computer? Who sent them off to the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Any of the operators. Usually the one who would reproduce it type it in and encrypt it. That person would send it off and note down in the log that that task was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you about that log a little bit later. Can you tell me now, did you work with the army unit that were at the site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were in the same building. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe what -- what -- just briefly what kind of cooperation you had in terms of sharing information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: At one point when I and their chief met in the facility it was assumed that we were doing the same job. Then in the beginning we started to agree on certain things. Later when the information became more important I then suggested that we could exchange information and send the information together, both to one and the other centre with the assumption that it would be useful. So in that period we exchanged or collated the information, which would then be sent by them to their centre and I would be sending this information to my centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you yourself take part in the actual listening and taping and transcribing and typing of -- of intercept conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. At one stage, this was in June and July, there was a need, not just for me to be there, but for at least five more people to be there, which we didn't have, so I really spent a lot of time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in my office have I recently provided you with 11 intercepts of your -- of your printout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to confirm that you had -- you had been the person involved in obtaining those 11 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were you able to determine by looking at the -- the printout of the intercept that you were actually involved in the process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I have to say that, in the beginning, I formulated everything up there. I established it, and this is a thread that goes through all of our reports, with some small differences. At the end of the report I would put my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, was it your signature or your -- or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, there was a number which actually stood for my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's get just one of those reports so you can briefly explain how that worked. It is a 65 ter number 1074 -- sorry, I -- it is 65 ter number 20 -- PO2379B, an intercept dated 11 July 1995 at 1800 hours. If we could bring up that on the -- B on the -- on the -- just the B/C/S printout on the -- okay. Now, first of all, can you just start from the top and -- we can -- we all know at this point what CSB and SDB -- SDB is state security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the -- can you tell us what CSB is just so I'm -- I've never been clear on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that includes both the state security and the public security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we can see the date there, we can see that it's marked "very urgent" in English. You actually used English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No -- well, yes, in this case, yes. Because this is a term that we actually used in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see the word "broj" which ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does -- just what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That's the number of the report before that there are so many, that many reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you slowly read in -- in your language the -- the three lines below the number, 539?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. That's the formulation that we drafted that contains all the elements that are important for this conversation. "On the aforementioned day while monitoring radio relay in the Pale direction" - we named it that - "on frequency 836 megahertz at 1800 hours, we recorded a conversation between General Gvero and General Gobijara, whom we could not hear. General Gvero's responses are as follows."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to go through the intercept, but if we could scroll down to the -- to the bottom of this intercept, I guess we have to go to the next page. Okay. On this page we see the intercept finishing up, then we see a line. And then we see the numbers. Without telling us what these numbers are, we see a first set of numbers and a slash and then a second set of numbers. Can you tell us what the first set of numbers means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Those are call signs. Codes of the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does that -- that number, that first one we're looking at belong to someone, or identify one of you guys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If he's going to mention names, then we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, don't mention names, but if you could tell us who that belongs to, without -- without mentioning names, I think we're okay on this one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The first one is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is the second number one of your team members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the significance, if any, of those two numbers in that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We had introduced a rule to make it so, to involve two men on each document that was recorded, and later reproduced at that location. So according to that rule, based on our mutual agreement, the first person would record the conversation and the second one would type it up and possibly dispatch it to the centre. However, since it was all on one desk, both persons listened to the conversation and both of them took part in typing it up. It was simply inevitable, so we were practically working together. But the rule was that the first person who pressed the record button would be responsible for that part of the job, while the other one would do the typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've mentioned earlier that -- that these intercepts were noted in a log. I went to direct your attention, we have a -- a number PO2371, which is five pages of a photocopy of that log, but you -- you brought your original of that log today, didn't you? If you could open up that original to -- let's just open it up to the first intercept that we -- that we have been talking about, which is -- if you can find your number 539, and I think the ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could put that -- the original on the ELMO, it may be a little bit better to read, but I think we can also see number 539, it is about the sixth -- sixth one down in this -- in this photocopy. If we could zoom in a bit on -- on the -- with the ELMO to that top, about fifth line. No, he -- or to where you -- to where you find the -- this -- this particular intercept. Okay. You've pointed to a -- to 539 on your original log. Can you just go through these line or two or what -- and tell us what this logbook is doing, or the significance of these numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The first column contains the cardinal numbers, and they are not anywhere on the documents. The second column contains two numbers of each line. In this case, P -- 5094, and then after that we see 359. 5094 was a number that I got from the text processor. At that time I was using the Norton Commander, and I got it from the text processor. That number, together with our number on the document, is introduced in the encrypting programme, and after the encryption it got an eight digit number which was 11751938. And after that there is a column reflecting the time at which that information was dispatched through communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it must be a logistical problem, but I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the photocopy we received absolutely does not correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreter ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correspond to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that or I can't help you there. Mr. McCloskey, I suppose, can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it -- I -- I can't explain that right now, Mr. President, but I -- I think the book -- he's taken us to what is the appropriate spot, and we'll try to help counsel with that at the break and -- to see what the -- what the problem may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that satisfactory to you, Madam Fauveau? Is that satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It -- we're look -- the page we are looking at does actually correspond. I just refer you to down to the -- a little bit beyond the middle of the page, not the fifth line, like I kind of misdirected us to by accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you know what copy Madam Fauveau has in her hands? I suppose if you can tell us the ERN number, Madam Fauveau, Mr. McCloskey would be able to see clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could be 1385, the last four digits, and I think we're all got the same one. I just directed you to the fifth line at the top, and I was wrong; the witness has taken us down farther into the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Nikolic, until Madam Fauveau verifies.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, it does correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to point out a problem with the transcript. In line 15, I think the witness was talking about P instead of number 5. That can later create confusion when we analyse the transcript. That's from line 15 onwards. I think he was talking about the letter P instead of number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 15 of which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Page 15, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That changes everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And if we could go back to the document, I -- the document that I read that he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you go back to 539 and just confirm for us that that first number in the line is actually a -- is a letter P; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We see from the previous ones that it is a letter P. It's smudged a little at this line, but we see it's P094.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, can you tell us, once these -- the conversations were on the -- the UHER tape, as far as you know, were any of those conversations saved on -- any of the audio saved on tape in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: A lot of conversations that we appraised as interesting at that moment we tried to re-record on another tape from the UHER, and there were, on the other hand, other conversations that were less interesting, were not recorded on tape, because we didn't have enough tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this first conversation that we have been discussing, the 11 July one, had you recently had a chance to listen to an audiotape of that conversation in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did it correspond to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember we had a problem, and the problem was the beginning and the end of conversation; it was not on that recording. They were not on that recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation for how the beginning and the end didn't get on the recording that you were listening to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I have two explanations. One, that I made a mistake when I was doing that, when I was doing the dubbing, because towards the end when the gentleman who is speaking says, "So much" I thought he had finished, and that's when I stopped the recording, because I didn't have the transcript, so I wasn't able to follow. That's one option. And another possibility is that when dubbing was done from one UHER tape to another, the person who did the dubbing made the same mistake. And at the end of the day I don't know whether these recordings will reach you, but maybe we'll find out whether it was my mistake or somebody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you mentioned the possibility of your mistake, are you talking about something that you did this year to provide the OTP with the tape? You're not talking about the wartime period, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: When I speak about my mistake, I'm talking about the present day. My colleagues had given me a call to tell me you needed a recording and, since I knew that job better, they invited me to do the dubbing and maybe then I made it mistake of the but if I did, I think we'll know that before the end of this day. However, there is another possibility, namely that it happened when -- during dubbing from the big UHER tape to another tape, so the colleague let the tape run from the first part when they are exchange greetings and he continues recording until the moment when the speaker says "so much, that's it," as if he were ending the conversation, and there is indeed a pause after that. So that's another possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me then just move on to a -- a document that I showed you. I won't spend the time to get the document up, but it's a document dated 21 September 1995, and it -- it talks about damage to a -- I believe damage to an antenna at the northern site. And an investigation into how that happened. Can you just tell us briefly, as you did to me in my office, what -- what you think that was about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We had this problem about the quality of signal, and I realised that if I managed to find a better antenna I could improve the quality of the signal. Since it involved the frequency range also used by Telekom in one section, I managed to get a parabolic antenna from them and prepare it for installation. Since that area is very windy, subject to very strong winds, we had to be very careful about installation. And in that period the antenna, together with the fixtures used to fix it to that pillar, was sitting in an underground corridor. And when the time came to install it I noticed first that two of the components, two fixtures were missing, and I also noticed two holes made in the antenna, made with a sharp object. I was very angry, I found it very hard to understand how that could have happened, and walking around the area I found this sharp object, compared it to the holes made in the antenna, and I realised that the holes were consistent and I said the sharp object would be preserved as evidence and that the person found to be responsible would be punished. I knew of course that these holes would make no difference to the quality of receiving the signal, and I only mentioned keeping it as evidence in anger, but this was completely misinterpreted by -- by the army as reference to enemy activity. I managed to find new fixtures within a day and we managed to install the antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Reading your first statement, in fact your testimony before this Tribunal, in another case that I will not name now, I noticed that you said, among other things, that your unit, or your section, together with the other military unit, exchanged information on a daily basis. So I want to ask you, did that also happen in the period we are interested in; July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Particularly to that period, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were in daily contact -- in fact, you said you were in contact, and my question is, was it on a daily basis, with the head of that other military unit, with their commander? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of contact you mean. We saw each other every day, we were in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the exchange of information you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was not our duty to be in contact to exchange information. The exchange of information could have been handled by the operators because we ourselves were not there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that in a way you aggregated this information you had. Could you just clarify, does it involve comparing two versions recorded by two units, comparing words or clarifying certain words that one of you did not hear very well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No. When the report would already be typed up, transcribed in electronic form, we never corrected it. We never changed it. It went as it were, and every operator had to be responsible for his own work. We just united the reports, we just attached them together and sent them that way. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, about the notes that you made before you would transcribe information on a PC. If you were unable to hear certain things very well, did you try to clarify those things with the other unit at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I have to admit that we asked each other's assistance in some cases. If you want me to explain further, especially that was the case if a particular recording concerned a part of the range that was listened to mainly by them. And in that case we would ask them, did you get that recording and what is this, and we would get answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you exchanged it, they did the same with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, that couldn't go that way because they did not listen to our section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were doing really fine, Mr. Zivanovic, finishes his question, switches off his microphone so that no one can hear your voice, and you were answering. However, just for the last two questions you have been butting in straight away. So please allow a short pause between question and answer, okay? Mr. Zivanovic has been doing it, so it's you that we need now to comply. Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question that relates to the methods used by your division. Since you were the head of that unit, that whole work, did you organise work within your unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Let's go into private session, please. I don't see that we are in private session, as yet. I don't see that we are in open session either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had agreed, Mr. Zivanovic, that we would not mention in open session that he was the head of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I mean we are bound to make mistakes at least one a day. So that's forgiven. But let's redact that part, please. And let's go back to open session and proceed from there. And you can answer the question without mentioning that you were the head of that unit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I organised the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the operator, having heard that conversation, would either put it down on a piece of paper or would transcribe it directly into the computer, if the audibility was good?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: To make things quite clear, first he would record the conversation, and after that, if everything was perfectly audible, he would let the tape run and transcribe it on the computer. If the workload was too large, then he would do the transcribing later, not straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have notebooks so that you would write in notebooks, copied from those pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We didn't need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you organise work in that way? For expediency or for what reason? Because it must have taken a lot of time to copy from paper to the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, we did not have notebooks in the first place, and we had no need to preserve written copies. We didn't need to preserve it in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, you have explained that. You explained also that there were two persons per shift in your unit. Did you work around the clock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were there, in fact, two persons were there five to seven days a week, and they were there as long as the -- there were activities going on. You know that people do not talk all the time. There are intervals in between conversations so that people would eat and drink in the meantime and sometimes conversations would take place very late. One operator could remain on duty until 3.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to know something else. Was the work of operators organised in shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No. They were there together all the time. With the proviso that after midnight, if traffic had stopped, one of them could go to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed among other things that you had a black notebook, it was mentioned in one of your statements. Do you still have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It's a black agenda, and I just showed you a report from that black agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your private agenda or is it a service book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It is still in the safe-keeping of the company where I work. It's not private.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So I suppose that the data recorded there are some sort of official secret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if approval had been given to disclose this agenda before this Tribunal in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: What the investigators had requested and what they had photocopies was agreed and approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean the rest wasn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether, after the time that has elapsed, it is still secret. I would have to get briefed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about this antenna. If I understood you properly, until it was damaged, before that, the antenna wasn't used at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, we didn't use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had antennas that you were using in your work. Can you please tell me whether these antennas were also used by this other unit that was at the same facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We had separate antennas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. This antenna that you repaired and set up. It stayed at the facility and you continued to use it until the end, let's say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it remained there and perhaps it's still there. I never checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Meek. Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. We have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You explained about the coding of the operators on each document that would be dispatched from your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that the participants -- or actually the operators who worked on the intercepts wrote their names at the bottom of the document, at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So there -- it wasn't -- the application of codes was not a rule that was constantly applied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it was a rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And why did it happen then that some of the operators put their actual names on the document, whether it was the typist or the person who intercepted the conversation? Why was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I will try to explain. On the 25th of May, 1995, two of my colleagues were wounded in Tuzla. It's a shell that is widely known about, which is killed 71 people. On that occasion they were wounded. At that point in time I was two men short, and since we were in the Security Services centre together, there is the public security centre there, so we asked the then minister requesting him to lend us two people with that professional profile who would come to that location and continue the work. It was desirable that those people have certain qualifications and that is how we got two people from the Security Services centre who came to our section. Since they were not a member of the service they did not have their own codes, but signed themselves with their proper name. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So that means that those people were part of some sort of reserve force in a way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You didn't understand me properly. They were active employees of the public Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I understand now. Thank you. Just one more question. Regarding the monitoring of the frequencies during your earlier testimony and during today's testimony you said you monitoring the frequency of the Main Staff. Was that your primary frequency that you were monitoring during your work during the -- at the northern location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you listen in to other frequencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you were identifying the speakers, the participants, and when you testified about this before you gave an explanation of how this could be done, how they could be identified, meaning the names and then how this later was transferred to the computer. In certain cases, if you did not note down the names of the participants on a piece of paper or if this was not entered directly into the computer, how were you able to identify the speakers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't understand you properly. If we identified them we would note that down. If we did not identify them, we would mark them as X and Y, name unknown. And there are plenty of reports like that. If we did not hear what the name was, we would put the question mark next to the name, indicating that we were not sure that it was that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1101? This is at tab 2. A is in English and B is in B/C/S, and could we please show this to the witness in B/C/S? Can we please zoom in a little bit on the document? Thank you. Sir, could you please look at the text of this intercept. I was not able to conclude how you managed to identify the conversation between a certain Krstic. How did you identify this name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It's like this: We know it's Krstic but I don't know who Krstic is. At that point in time I don't know who it is, so I used the term "a certain Krstic" and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. How I identified it, well, I would have to read it to just refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: As we can see, Krstic is not mentioned anywhere, and I wrote that down. That's the problem I see. When the connection was put through, sometimes it would happen that the operator would say who is asking to speak with whom. Sometimes it would also happen in view of the fact this was not a frequency that we listened to a lot. At the point in when I got there, I heard it and then I depressed the pause button, so this was not recorded. Then I would note down that this was a certain Krstic speaking with Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. This is what I heard. Otherwise how or why I would write it, I wasn't making it up. There is no reason for me to make it up. There must have been some kind of indication.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Then we don't have the lieutenant-colonel as the text goes on in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but probably while listening to previous intercepts we knew that it was the lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Although you were not listening to that frequency very often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, we didn't listen to it very often, but there is the possibility that the switchboard operator said such and such a rank person or that he said the lieutenant-colonel would like to speak with such and such a person.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But since you didn't monitor that frequency a lot, this is some sort of assumption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, it's not an assumption. It cannot be an assumption if I wrote it down. I did not dare assume anything, and I had no reason to make assumptions about anything, because -- I don't know how to explain it to you. We didn't need assumptions of any kind in our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have the break now. Because of the redaction it needs to be 30 minutes. And Judge Kwon has arrived, and he'll be joining us after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Defence team for Mr. Borovcanin. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the northern location that we mentioned earlier, and according to what we know, there were two military units there. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we just move into private session, Your Honours, Because I wanted to refer to one of the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to now ask you about the exchange of intercepts between you and this military unit. When I say you, I'm thinking of the people from the service that you belonged to. Did it ever happen that one intercept that was recorded both by the military unit and yourselves was different, that there were differences in the text, in the names, in the numbers, in the geographic names, and in other features?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. When I say this, you really need to keep in mind that we did not analyse the intercepts. We were just an operations department that would pass them on. I don't know if things like that were found when these intercepts were being analysed in the appropriate section. I don't know. But there is the possibility. When I say there is the possibility, then in the technical aspect a radio relay connection has the so-called frequency of one participant and the duplex frequency of the other participant. And what can happen is that we listen to the first and didn't hear the second one. There is the possibility that they heard the second one and perhaps the first one as well. There were such cases and, amongst other examples, you have the previous intercept there where we did not hear the second participant. Somebody maybe was able to hear the second participant. I know that at one point we had that problem with this frequency that we were listening in to, until we also found the duplex frequency. So then listening to the main frequency, and we had a quality signal there, then combined with the telephone connection we could hear the second speaker without using the duplex frequency. I hope you are satisfied with the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you this is, if you noticed a certain difference in the geographical names or the names of the collocutors, you would take the same intercept that you already listened to, also from the army. And then did you send both the intercepts in their original version to your superior section?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: They were always sent in their original version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you up there at the position never compared the two intercepts or did anything with them, but you would send both of them off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. They were always both sent off. I have to clarify one thing, just for a second. If we reproduced a conversation that the army was intensively listening to and it was important to us, but we were unable to recognise the speakers because they did not introduce themselves, at sometime we would ask them to come and listen to that intercept and since you're listening to that constantly, "Can you say who that is," and then they would say, "That is such and such a person, 100 per cent." So in such cases when the information was important, we would do that. When it was very important for us to know the names, if you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am trying to. But let's try to give an example of this. You heard a conversation, you felt that it was very important, you were unable to recognise the speakers. You would call somebody from the army, they would come and say, "We are constantly monitoring this person, we are familiar with his characteristics, the vocabulary he uses; it's Zivanovic."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, in the typewritten text that you would send to your superior service, would you write in how you identified a participant, for example a participant like Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I know one thing 100 per cent. Any -- every report that came from the military we would write that it was received from the 2nd Corps Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit. I know this for a fact. When we would call, for example, the operator who would be listening in to Zivanovic and he said, "This is Zivanovic," in that case we wouldn't write that in. It didn't mean that much to us. We were doing that for our own purposes, we didn't know at that time that we would be coming here and explaining our methods of work. Otherwise we would have written it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So in such situations, you would say the speaker is Zivanovic. You didn't know that information, but you received it from somebody from the army, and then he would send that off in that way to your superior service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, you could say it was like that, but again I say this is something that was done very infrequently. In essence the participants were not that important to us. What was important to us was the actual content of the conversation, the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this here, even though I didn't mean to ask that. Why do you believe that the participants were not important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, let me try to explain. If in the report there was talk about how something was going to happen in a certain sector, at that moment that was the main thing. Who said that at that particular time, basically, was not important to us. Perhaps it was more important to the military, but in the operations sense it wasn't important for us. What was important was to know what was being prepared and what would happen in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But can we agree that if in the conversation it was said such and such a person is coming with his unit, it's important to know the name of the person because that way you could identify the unit, the strength of the unit, the capacity of the unit. So for somebody who was listening to that, the name would be an important thing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: As I said, it was probably more important to know that if you were in the military rather than in the intelligence service. The army was using and moving and positioning units in these places. As far as we were concerned we were not doing that; so for us, the actual data, the intelligence was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Counsel, and Witness, please slow down a little bit. I figured out that the interpreters are finding it a little bit difficult to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will try to slow down as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Today in response to a question by the Prosecutor, as well as in the proofing notes that we received from the Prosecution, you mentioned the event from the 21st of September, 1995 [Realtime transcript read in error "2005"], when this equipment was damaged. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I remember the damage, but I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the transcript, I would like to say again that I said the 21st of September, 1995, and on page 34, line 23, the date is the 21st of September, 2005. So I would just like to make a correction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So just leaving aside the date, my question is, who could have caused the damage on that equipment at that location at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really don't know who it was. I was angry at the time and I wanted to express my state of mind, my mood. I don't know. I don't know. To this very day I don't know, I didn't even know that there was a report made on this, and that it was qualified as a hostile or enemy activity. I think that's what it says. This is something that is specific to the military. Soldiers know that in wartime many things can be qualified differently than we as civilians would qualify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the damage could have been caused either by somebody by the army or your own service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There was nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at your proofing notes I come to the conclusion that one of your explanations was that it could have been done by the army, motivated by envy or malice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You know, up there on that location it was a struggle for the best possible signal. Engineers competed in installing aerials, and I was lucky to have a knowledgeable friend. And when I finally managed to get hold of that parabolic antenna, maybe somebody was a petty spirit, envious enough to do something like that. Or maybe somebody had a beer too many and did that. But I really didn't realise it was such a terrible problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next topic, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, Your Honour. We have finished with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you concerns the tapes you used. Did it occur that tapes and intercepts recorded in longhand before they were taken, before they were sent to your service, would be collected by you and then transcribed together in your own centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No. Everything was done on that location, and from that location we sent it all to the centre through communications. In fact, I have to add, in order to be completely clear, there were cases when a conversation was in English, and I seem to remember that in one or two cases we invited an interpreter to our location and yet in another couple of cases we had to take the intercept concerned to our service for it to be translated there. That's all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this for the following reason: Another witness is scheduled to appear, a witness from your service speaking on that topic, and since I don't have any further opportunity to speak to you, I want to read out this passage from his testimony. "In rare occasions when he was present," meaning you, "and a very important conversation was being intercepted, he would take the handwritten copy and the tape to the base to transcribe them there." So when would that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know how many cases like that we had, but they always concerned something that had to be taken to Sarajevo immediately. There were a few intercepts, and I really can't remember, it was very long ago, but we had to take the audiorecording as well. If something like that could have been sent just in written form, then it would have been. However, the tape and the written transcription would be taken to Sarajevo immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you mean that this witness refers to these cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, and they were very, very rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In November 2003 you testified before this Tribunal in another case. And you were asked about the tapes you used. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't remember the question exactly, but of course I testified about tapes as well. If you can remind me, I will answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you very briefly. What happened to those tapes? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I think I've spoken about this already. First we had a problem with the tapes, we did not have enough of them. For that reason it was our call which intercepts would be dubbed on to one large tape, marking the precise times of the beginning and the end of each intercept. We did that with extremely important intercepts. I know we did that. When you ask me about the fate of the tapes, I hope you understand my role in all of that. Such intercepts were taken to the headquarters where there were people who were doing that part of the job, and in addition to using the information from the tapes they were also in charge of safe keeping the tapes. So they were no longer in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From that moment on you have no information about those tapes, you don't know if they are still in existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Just by chance I happen to know about a part of them. Recently when the OTP asked that part of some intercepts be re-recorded, they invited me, as a member of the service, who knew his way around those tapes, to do that job, and I know that those intercepts that were requested are still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me get this clear. Those were recordings that you made, not the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single intercept among those shown to you and asked about by the Prosecutor that was re-recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I know about one of them because I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask the Court to go into private session for the last couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. West [phoen] testified here, we had occasion to see certain documents mentioning the name of Pasaga Mesic. My question is, do you know who he is, Pasaga Mesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that at that time, meaning July 1995, he was the head of the service that employed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not hear. What I would like to know is when you reproduced the conversations of the 2nd Corps, did you have a possibility to listen to the tapes they had, or did you only receive the report? Did you only receive the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was not I who transcribed the intercepts originating from the 2nd Corps. I received that in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You had no -- you had no opportunity to hear the tape on which this was registered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I did not need to listen to it. It would have been too much for us. We were having difficulty coping with our part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since you didn't have an opportunity to check these tapes, you can't say that the report you received corresponded exactly to the conversation which had been taped; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I didn't give it any thought. I thought those men were doing their job well, and we just accepted it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you transmitted one of your reports to the army you did not transmit also the tape, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct. I did not send the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said, therefore, that tape made by the army of which you received the report, was indeed sent to your superiors, and also to the superiors of the 2nd Corps which were on the same site as you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I can assert that that tape was not sent to my service. Where it was sent, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think there's been a mistake. I will repeat my question. The report of a conversation, an intercept intercepted by the army for which you received the report, you sent it to your superiors, your -- your supervisors, your superiors, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the army sent these reports to their own superiors, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So the conversation was intercepted only once, but two reports left and concerned the same intercept. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke a while ago -- or perhaps a question was asked of you about the 21st Division, and you said that you didn't have any knowledge of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D168, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the document is arriving, but I could give you a paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the number correct? 5D168, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see on this document whether it is indeed a document which left from your place, which was sent from your place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see on this document that it came from the 21st Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this help you? Does this help you to remember that there was a 21st Division on the same site as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, that means nothing to me. I really didn't deal in those matters. These things didn't matter to me. I called them PEB of the 2nd Corps, and for the 21st Division, I really didn't notice that or didn't pay attention maybe, I don't know. It's obviously a document that we had forwarded, having received it from the PEB, the entire Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit of the 21st Division, and sent it on to our centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true -- is it true that you used the computer of the army to send your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There was a period when we did not have the technical facilities to forward information from our location to the centre. At that time we requested from our colleagues in the PEB of the 2nd Corps to let us -- or rather to do the forwarding through their own communications. Since these two centres were physically very close, every time that such information would arrive, the operator would put it on a diskette, inform an employee of my service at the headquarters, and that person would come and fetch them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When your report left from the army computer, was it a person from your service who was working on the army computer or was it an army personnel who was taking your data and used this computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We had a computer on our location, but at one stage we did not have the technical facilities to send information, due to the fact that the modem was broken or something. So we would physically give them the information on a diskette and their signalsman would send it on. And I don't rule out the possibility that you raised; maybe that happened. Maybe. I cannot remember every moment and every day. I cannot claim now that the computer was always working. Maybe my operator would really go once in a while to the PEB centre of the 2nd Corps and dictate what he had to say. I cannot rule out the possibility, but even if it happened, it happened in the way I'm describing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: About the tapes, you said that you didn't have enough tapes. Is it true that you reused the same tapes and that you would record on an already recorded tape, over the previous conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I have said that already, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did it sometimes happen when you reused the same tape, the previous conversation wasn't completely erased and indeed on the new registration you could hear parts of the previous conversation or intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, if you have any knowledge about the way recordings are made, you will understand that regardless of whether something is deleted or not, erased or not, every new recording erases what was there previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown document 5D172. THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: We didn't hear properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D172, and it is indeed in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is indeed an intercept which you took from the 2nd Corps; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true if you looked at the second intercept, which was taped at 2107 [ass interpreted], there is a sentence which says that IHR did not properly erase the previous conversation; in consequence, EY is practically inaudible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That never happened to me. You would have to ask the operator who recorded this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, this sentence, it's from the 2nd Corps that -- you had it. You didn't add this sentence, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that even when you sent or transported the tapes yourself to your headquarters, it was not originals, but when you had very important tapes you would put them on -- several tapes, you would re-record them on a bigger tape, on a new tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Both occurred. I explained a moment ago that if something was very important, I explained the procedure, how I took it directly to the centre. And other conversations were recorded on a compilation tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. On line 21 on the previous page, page 43, 2107 should read 2137. Yes, Madam Fauveau, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago you spoke about intercepts in English. An English intercept, was it first typed in its original version in English or was it first translated in your language and then transcribed on the computer at your site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I know that it was immediately translated into our language. Whether, when it was taken to the company, it was typed up in English, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, if there were a mistake in a translation, a mistranslation, this mistake would appear in the report of the transcription which was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: An error in translation would be due to the translator. I really couldn't explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke a while ago of this notebook where you entered information concerning the report which was transmitted. Who was in charge of putting the information in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Nobody in particular was in charge of that. Those who were dealing with a particular piece of information had the duty to enter in this logbook the elements that were envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So, if I understand correctly, the people who were able to send the information were the ones who were actually entering the information in that notebook; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, as a record of dispatched information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And after the war, that notebook, was it archived somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us, before coming here to court, where did you take this notebook from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: From the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have clearance from your government to give this information? Because if you don't, I will not let you disclose it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I already provided parts of the logbook from previous cases, for them to be copied, I brought it in case I needed to refresh my memory in case I was asked something so that I don't do that on the basis of my recollection, but that I have that to refer back to. It's a standard log, and other than the number of the information, nothing else should be confidential. So I can show the report and that it was logged in and that it was dispatched from the location to the destination where our centre was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we please go to a closed session for just one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you monitored the headquarters through one of your machines. Can you tell us, when did you start monitoring that frequency, the headquarters of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I cannot remember the specific date, but I think that we managed to find that frequency in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us if you looked for that frequency or you just found it completely by chance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We found it accidentally, but we wanted to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And before finding that frequency, did you really try hard to find it? Were you looking for it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-128: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
